rotations.name: Current: soybean then fallow
rotations.farmer_summary: Soybean grows in the wet summer, then the field stays empty and loses water through the dry months.
rotations.why: Your current plan as described: soybean sown in October and harvested around February, then fallow.
evidence: Water balance is positive in every soybean month, from +36.4 mm in February to +124.3 mm in December.
Water balance is negative in the fallow months, reaching -21.8 mm in July.
NDVI in February reaches 0.59, showing dense crop cover during soybean.
rotations.temperature_fit: Monthly means of 24.1 to 25.1 °C from October to February sit inside the soybean range of 20-30 °C.
benefits: Matches the wet season and uses the summer rain well
risks: Field stays bare or fallow for about 7 months and loses water
Soybean has low drought tolerance if the rain fails
general_knowledge: Leaving the soil uncovered in the dry season can increase evaporation and erosion.

rotations.name: Soybean then sorghum
rotations.farmer_summary: Soybean in summer, then sorghum sown after harvest that tolerates dry weather and uses less water.
rotations.why: Sorghum is the top-ranked second crop and has high drought tolerance, so it keeps the soil in use after soybean with less water.
evidence: Water balance is -26.0 mm in April and -15.4 mm in May, the main dry-period deficit for sorghum.
Rain in February totals 160.9 mm, enough to establish sorghum after soybean.
NDVI in February is 0.59, showing the field is green when sorghum is sown.
rotations.temperature_fit: February sowing at 24.1 °C fits the 21-35 °C range, but May at 20.0 °C and June at 19.3 °C fall below ideal during the late cycle.
benefits: High drought tolerance for the dry months
Covers the soil in the period that is bare in the current plan
risks: Late cycle falls into a water deficit and cooler weather
Sorghum has lower market value than soybean
general_knowledge: Sorghum is commonly used for grain or silage in Brazil.

rotations.name: Soybean then cowpea
rotations.farmer_summary: Soybean in summer, then cowpea sown in February, a short crop that tolerates dry conditions and fixes nitrogen.
rotations.why: Cowpea is a short-cycle legume with high drought tolerance, so it covers part of the dry season with a low water need.
evidence: Water balance is -26.0 mm in April, the deficit that cowpea must cope with at the end of its cycle.
Water balance is +36.4 mm in February, a surplus when cowpea is sown.
NDVI in February is 0.59, showing green cover at sowing.
rotations.temperature_fit: February and March means of 24.1 °C sit inside the 22-32 °C range, but May at 20.0 °C is below the ideal minimum.
benefits: Short cycle of about 75 days with high drought tolerance
Fixes nitrogen and adds organic matter
risks: Harvest in May can face cooler, drier weather
Leaves June to September without cover
general_knowledge: Cowpea grain has good local market demand in parts of Brazil.

recommendation.message_to_farmer: Sow sorghum in February, right after the soybean harvest, when the rain is strong, with February rainfall about 160.9 mm. Sorghum tolerates dry weather and uses less water than a second soybean crop. The trade-off is that its late cycle in May and June runs into cooler weather and a water deficit, and sorghum usually earns less than soybean. Your local rain onset is typically around 9 October, so sowing soybean in October fits the usual calendar. Please confirm the dates and yield with a local agronomist before deciding.

disclaimer: Based on NASA POWER and MODIS satellite estimates at a 50 km grid, which may differ from your field. Monthly data covers only 2020-2024. The irrigation signal is not detected. Please validate with a local agronomist.
